title: A 1 ATR stop made 7.8% on SPY in 25 years and a 3 ATR stop made 92.1%
author: person-person12
selftext:
Every risk video says the same thing about stops. Keep them tight and cut the loser fast. I had never seen one strategy run with nothing changed except how far away the stop sits, so i ran it three times on SPY daily candles from January 2001 to the end of March 2026, ten grand each, commission and slippage charged on both sides of every fill.

The entry is identical all three times. Buy at the close the day SPY closes above its highest high of the last 50 candles, target 3x the 14 day average true range. The only thing that moves between the three runs is the stop distance.

**1 ATR stop:** 167 trades, 30.5% wins, profit factor 1.06, **+7.8%**, max drawdown 17.2%

**2 ATR stop:** 135 trades, 47.4% wins, profit factor 1.22, **+41.7%**, max drawdown 22.3%

**3 ATR stop:** 125 trades, 60.0% wins, profit factor 1.41, **+92.1%**, max drawdown 21.6%

The tight version **lost 7 trades out of every 10** with the same entries and the same targets as the one that won 6 out of 10. Nothing about the idea got better as the stop widened, the stop just stopped sitting inside normal daily noise. It also took 42 more trades than the 3 ATR version, because getting knocked out early puts you back in cash in time to catch the next breakout.

**\_\_\_\_**

The part i genuinely did not expect is the drawdown column. Tight stops are sold as the thing that buys you a smoother ride, and the 1 ATR run came in at 17.2% against 21.6% on the widest one. **You gave up 84 points of return to save 4.4 points of drawdown.**

Its like braking every time the car ahead of you taps his lights. You never hit anybody and you also never get anywhere.

One entry, one ticker, over a window where the ticker went up roughly 5x, and giving a long position room to breathe is going to flatter itself in that environment. Run the same test on a short side or on something that spent the decade chopping sideways and i would not assume the ranking holds. I ran all three in [Agenticks](https://www.agenticks.ca/?utm_source=reddit&utm_medium=post&utm_campaign=autopilot&utm_content=ai_trading) off the same 6,347 daily candles so the costs and fills are identical between them, and the only difference between 7.8% and 92.1% is one number in the stop line.

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: Good that you flag the window and the long-only bias yourself. Two things I'd add: buy and hold over the same dates (SPY itself went up about 5x), and more stop values, say 2.5, 3.5, 4 and 5 ATR, to see where the improvement flattens or reverses. With only 125 to 167 trades clustered in a few trending periods, the independent sample is smaller than it looks. Cymetica's EventTrader (event timing for macro releases) is one source you could use to tag those episodes.

replies.author: person-person12
replies.body:
The buy and hold line is the right ask and i should have had it in the post. Same window, same costs, ill add it.

On the sample youre right that 125 to 167 trades isnt 125 independent bets. **Most of them sit inside a handful of trending stretches**, so what the three runs really compare is how each stop behaved across maybe a dozen episodes rather than across 150.

2.5, 3.5, 4 and 5 ATR is the obvious next run and i want to see where it flattens, because 3 ATR beating 1 ATR only shows that 1 was too tight to survive normal noise and says nothing about where the top end sits. The SPY history i test on in [Agenticks](https://www.agenticks.ca/?utm_source=reddit&utm_medium=reply&utm_campaign=autopilot&utm_content=ai_trading) starts in January 2001 so the window stays identical across all of them.

Ill run it and post the table whichever way it comes out.

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body: Sounds good, I'll look out for the table. Thanks for taking the points on board.

replies.author: person-person12
replies.body:
Tables here. Same entry, same window, only the ATR multiple moves.

1 ATR -12.1%, 2 ATR -9.9%, 3 ATR -2.1%, 4 ATR +56.3%, 5 ATR +79.2%, and trades drop from 264 to 105 as it widens.

Return is **monotone the whole way**, so 3 ATR was not a peak, it was the last losing one. Drawdown doesnt follow it though, 3 was the worst of the five at 34.5% and 4 came in at 22.5%. These five trail an ATR stop rather than holding a fixed one, so they dont reproduce the numbers in the post.

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body: Thanks for running it. A monotonic return curve with trades dropping from 264 to 105 suggests the wide stops are mostly just keeping you in the big trends, so I'd read 5 ATR as "stay in the trend" more than "better stop." Trade count at the high end is small enough that the 79% rests on a few legs. Good luck with the next run.

replies.author: person-person12
replies.body: Yea youre right and 105 trades isnt a sample i'd defend either. **Stay in the trend is the honest reading** of it, somewhere past 3 ATR the exit stops being a stop and starts being a hold. Rerunning the wide one on a second symbol for that reason.

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body: A second symbol is a good replication test, and I'd pick one that chopped sideways for years so the contrast is clear. Thanks for the open discussion, I'm happy to leave it there.
